name: Question 12
problem:
Suppose that $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for $s>a.$ Then, $F(s)$ is differentiable at every point $s>a,$ and we have

$$
{F}^{′}(s)=-\,L{t\cdot f(t)}.
$$

A proof of this statement is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ $F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t$ exists for $s>a.$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${F}^{′}(s)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${F}^{′}(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{∂}{∂s}({e}^{-st}f(t))\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $\frac{∂}{∂s}({e}^{-st}f(t))=-t{e}^{-st}f(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${F}^{′}(s)=-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }t{e}^{-st}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${F}^{′}(s)=-L{t\cdot f(t)}$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ and
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ and
{{field-3}}.
worked_solution:
If a function $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on $[0,\infty )$ and has exponential order $a,$ then its Laplace transform

$$
F(s)=L{f(t)}
$$

exists for every real $s>a,$ and $F$ is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence. 

The smoothness property states that, for each integer $n\ge 0$ and $s>a,$ we have

$$
{F}^{(n)}(s)=(-1)^{n}\,L{{t}^{n}f(t)}.
$$

We're asked to prove the smoothness property in the case $n=1.$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L2}.$ From line $\text{L1}$ we know that

$$
F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt.
$$

By $\text{the definition of the derivative with respect to }s$, we get

$$
{F}^{′}(s)=\frac{d}{ds}F(s)=\frac{d}{ds}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt,
$$

which is exactly the statement in line $\text{L2}.$

- Next we consider line $\text{L5}.$ From line $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
{F}^{′}(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{∂}{∂s}({e}^{-st}f(t))\,dt.
$$

Line $\text{L4}$ tells us that

$$
\frac{∂}{∂s}({e}^{-st}f(t))=-t{e}^{-st}f(t).
$$

Substituting this expression into the integrand in line $\text{L3}$ gives

$$
{F}^{′}(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }(-t{e}^{-st}f(t))\,dt=-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }t{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt.
$$

Therefore, line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{substitution}.$

- Finally, we consider line $\text{L6}.$ By $\text{the definition of the Laplace transform},$

$$
L{t\cdot f(t)}={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}(tf(t))\,dt.
$$

Comparing this with the integral in line $\text{L5}$, we see that

$$
{F}^{′}(s)=-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }t{e}^{-st}f(t)\,dt=-{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}(tf(t))\,dt=-\,L{t\cdot f(t)},
$$

which is exactly the expression in line $\text{L6}.$

EXPLANATION

If a function f(t) is piecewise continuous on [0,∞) and has exponential order a, then its Laplace transform F(s)=L{f(t)} exists for every real s>a, and F is infinitely differentiable in this region of convergence.

The smoothness property states that, for each integer n≥0 and s>a, we have F(n)(s)=(−1)nL{tnf(t)}.

We're asked to prove the smoothness property in the case n=1.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider line L2. From line L1 we know that F(s)=∫0∞e−stf(t)dt. By the definition of the derivative with respect to s, we get F′(s)=ddsF(s)=dds∫0∞e−stf(t)dt, which is exactly the statement in line L2.

  • Next we consider line L5. From line L3 we have F′(s)=∫0∞∂∂s(e−stf(t))dt. Line L4 tells us that ∂∂s(e−stf(t))=−te−stf(t). Substituting this expression into the integrand in line L3 gives F′(s)=∫0∞(−te−stf(t))dt=−∫0∞te−stf(t)dt. Therefore, line L5 follows from lines L3 and L4 by substitution.

  • Finally, we consider line L6. By the definition of the Laplace transform, L{t⋅f(t)}=∫0∞e−st(tf(t))dt. Comparing this with the integral in line L5, we see that F′(s)=−∫0∞te−stf(t)dt=−∫0∞e−st(tf(t))dt=−L{t⋅f(t)}, which is exactly the expression in line L6.
